This is a list of articles about [[prime number]]s. A prime number (or ''prime'') is a [[natural number]] greater than 1 that has no [[divisor]]s other than 1 and itself. By [[Euclid's theorem]], there is an infinite number of prime numbers. Subsets of the prime numbers may be generated with various [[formulas for primes]]. 

The first 1,000 primes are listed below, followed by lists of notable types of prime numbers in alphabetical order, giving their respective first terms. The number 1 is [[primality of 1|neither prime nor composite]].

== The first 1,000 prime numbers ==
The following table lists the first 1,000 primes, with 20 columns of consecutive primes in each of the 50 rows.<ref>{{Cite book | last = Lehmer | first = D. {{OEIS|A000040}}.

The [[Goldbach's conjecture|Goldbach conjecture]] verification project reports that it has computed all primes smaller than 4×10{{sup|18}}.<ref>Tomás Oliveira e Silva, [http://www.ieeta.pt/~tos/goldbach.html Goldbach conjecture verification] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110524084452/http://www.ieeta.pt/~tos/goldbach.html |date=24 May 2011 }}. Retrieved 16 July 2013</ref> That means 95,676,260,903,887,607 primes<ref>{{OEIS|id=A080127}}</ref> (nearly 10{{sup|17}}), but they were not stored. There are known formulae to evaluate the [[prime-counting function]] (the number of primes smaller than a given value) faster than computing the primes. This has been used to compute that there are 1,925,320,391,606,803,968,923 primes (roughly 2{{e|21}}) smaller than 10{{sup|23}}. A different computation found that there are 18,435,599,767,349,200,867,866 primes (roughly 2{{e|22}}) smaller than 10{{sup|24}}, if the [[Riemann hypothesis]] is true.<ref name="Franke">{{cite web|title=Conditional Calculation of pi(10{{sup|24}})|url=http://primes.utm.edu/notes/pi(10%5E24).html|author=Jens Franke|date=29 July 2010|access-date=17 May 2011|url-status=live|archive-url=http://archive.wikiwix.com/cache/20140824032441/http://primes.utm.edu/notes/pi(10%5E24).html|archive-date=24 August 2014}}</ref>

== Lists of primes by type ==
Below are listed the first prime numbers of many named forms and types. More details are in the article for the name. ''n'' is a [[natural number]] (including 0) in the definitions.

=== Balanced primes ===
{{main|Balanced prime}}
Balanced primes are primes with equal-sized [[Prime gap|prime gaps]] before and after them, making them the [[arithmetic mean]] of their next larger and next smaller prime.

* [[5 (number)|5]], [[53 (number)|53]], [[157 (number)|157]], [[173 (number)|173]], [[211 (number)|211]], [[257 (number)|257]], [[263 (number)|263]], 373, 563, 593, 607, 653, 733, 947, 977, 1103, 1123, 1187, 1223, 1367, 1511, 1747, 1753, 1907, 2287, 2417, 2677, 2903, 2963, 3307, 3313, 3637, 3733,   4013, 4409, 4457, 4597, 4657, 4691, 4993, 5107, 5113, 5303, 5387, 5393  ({{OEIS2C|A006562}}).

=== Bell primes ===
{{see also|Bell number#Bell primes}}
Bell primes are primes that are also the number of [[Partition of a set|partitions]] of some finite set.

[[2]], [[5]], [[877 (number)|877]], 27644437, 35742549198872617291353508656626642567, 359334085968622831041960188598043661065388726959079837.
The next term has 6,539 digits. ({{OEIS2C|A051131}})

=== Chen primes ===
{{main|Chen prime}}
Chen primes are primes ''p'' such that ''p''+2 is either a prime or [[semiprime]].

[[2]], [[3]], [[5]], [[7]], [[11 (number)|11]], [[13 (number)|13]], [[17 (number)|17]], [[19 (number)|19]], [[23 (number)|23]], [[29 (number)|29]], [[31 (number)|31]], [[37 (number)|37]], [[41 (number)|41]], [[47 (number)|47]], [[53 (number)|53]], [[59 (number)|59]], [[67 (number)|67]], [[71 (number)|71]], [[83 (number)|83]], [[89 (number)|89]], [[101 (number)|101]], [[107 (number)|107]], [[109 (number)|109]], [[113 (number)|113]], [[127 (number)|127]], [[131 (number)|131]], [[137 (number)|137]], [[139 (number)|139]], [[149 (number)|149]], [[157 (number)|157]], [[167 (number)|167]], [[179 (number)|179]], [[181 (number)|181]], [[191 (number)|191]], [[197 (number)|197]], [[199 (number)|199]], [[211 (number)|211]], [[227 (number)|227]], [[233 (number)|233]], [[239 (number)|239]], [[251 (number)|251]], [[257 (number)|257]], [[263 (number)|263]], [[269 (number)|269]], [[281 (number)|281]], [[293 (number)|293]], 307, 311, 317, 337, [[347 (number)|347]], [[353 (number)|353]], 359, 379, 389, 401, 409 ({{OEIS2C|A109611}})

=== Circular primes ===
{{main|Circular prime}}
A circular prime is a number that remains prime on any cyclic rotation of its base 10 digits.

[[2]], [[3]], [[5]], [[7]], [[11 (number)|11]], [[13 (number)|13]], [[17 (number)|17]], [[31 (number)|31]], [[37 (number)|37]], [[71 (number)|71]], [[73 (number)|73]], [[79 (number)|79]], [[97 (number)|97]], [[113 (number)|113]], [[131 (number)|131]], [[197 (number)|197]], [[199 (number)|199]], 311, 337, 373, 719, 733, 919, 971, 991, 1193, 1931, 3119, 3779, 7793, 7937, 9311, 9377, 11939, 19391, 19937, 37199, 39119, 71993, 91193, 93719, 93911, 99371, 193939, 199933, 319993, 331999, 391939, 393919, 919393, 933199, 939193, 939391, 993319, 999331 ({{OEIS2C|A068652}})

Some sources only include the smallest prime in each cycle. For example, listing 13, but omitting 31.

[[2]], [[3]], [[5]], [[7]], [[11 (number)|11]], [[13 (number)|13]], [[17 (number)|17]], [[37 (number)|37]], [[79 (number)|79]], [[113 (number)|113]], [[197 (number)|197]], [[199 (number)|199]], 337, 1193, 3779, 11939, 19937, 193939, 199933, 1111111111111111111, 11111111111111111111111 ({{OEIS2C|A016114}})

=== Cluster primes ===
{{main|Cluster prime}}
A cluster prime is a prime ''p'' such that every even [[natural number]] ''k'' ≤ ''p'' − 3 is the difference of two primes not exceeding ''p''.

[[3]], [[5]], [[7]], [[11 (number)|11]], [[13 (number)|13]], [[17 (number)|17]], [[19 (number)|19]], [[23 (number)|23]], ... ({{OEIS2C|A038134}})

All primes between 3 and 89, inclusive, are cluster primes. The first 10 primes that are ''not'' cluster primes are:

[[2]], [[97 (number)|97]], [[127 (number)|127]], [[149 (number)|149]], [[191 (number)|191]], [[211 (number)|211]], [[223 (number)|223]], [[227 (number)|227]], [[229 (number)|229]], [[251 (number)|251]].

=== Cousin primes ===
{{main|Cousin prime}}
{{see also|#Twin primes|#Prime triplets|#Prime quadruplets}}

Cousin primes are pairs of primes that differ by four.

([[3]], [[7]]), ([[7]], [[11 (number)|11]]), ([[13 (number)|13]], [[17 (number)|17]]), ([[19 (number)|19]], [[23 (number)|23]]), ([[37 (number)|37]], [[41 (number)|41]]), ([[43 (number)|43]], [[47 (number)|47]]), ([[67 (number)|67]], [[71 (number)|71]]), ([[79 (number)|79]], [[83 (number)|83]]), ([[97 (number)|97]], [[101 (number)|101]]), ([[103 (number)|103]], [[107 (number)|107]]), ([[109 (number)|109]], [[113 (number)|113]]), ([[127 (number)|127]], [[131 (number)|131]]), ([[163 (number)|163]], [[167 (number)|167]]), ([[193 (number)|193]], [[197 (number)|197]]), ([[223 (number)|223]], [[227 (number)|227]]), ([[229 (number)|229]], [[233 (number)|233]]), ([[277 (number)|277]], [[281 (number)|281]]) ({{OEIS2C|A023200}}, {{OEIS2C|A046132}})

=== Cuban primes ===
{{main|Cuban prime}}
Cuban primes are primes <math>p</math> of the form <math>p = k^3 - (k - 1)^3,</math> where <math>k</math> is a natural number.

The term is also used to refer to primes <math>p</math> of the form <math>p = (k^3 - (k - 2)^3)/2,</math> where <math>k</math> is a natural number.

[[13 (number)|13]], [[109 (number)|109]], [[193 (number)|193]], 433, 769, 1201, 1453, 2029, 3469, 3889, 4801, 10093, 12289, 13873, 18253, 20173, 21169, 22189, 28813, 37633, 43201, 47629, 60493, 63949, 65713, 69313, 73009, 76801, 84673, 106033, 108301, 112909, 115249 ({{OEIS2C|A002648}})

=== Cullen primes ===
{{main|Cullen number}}
Cullen primes are primes ''p'' of the form ''p''=''k''2{{sup|''k''}} + 1, for some natural number ''k''.

[[3]], 393050634124102232869567034555427371542904833 ({{OEIS2C|A050920}})

=== Delicate primes ===
{{main|Delicate prime}}
Delicate primes are those primes that always become a [[composite number]] when any of their base 10 digits is changed.

Mersenne primes are primes ''p'' of the form ''p'' = 2{{sup|''k''}} − 1, for some [[non-negative]] integer ''k''.

[[3]], [[7]], [[31 (number)|31]], [[127 (number)|127]], [[8191 (number)|8191]], [[131071 (number)|131071]], [[524287 (number)|524287]], [[2147483647]], 2305843009213693951, 618970019642690137449562111, 162259276829213363391578010288127, 170141183460469231731687303715884105727 ({{OEIS2C|A000668}})

{{As of|2024}}, there are 52 known Mersenne primes.<ref name="www.mersenne.org">{{Cite web |title=List of known Mersenne prime numbers - PrimeNet |url=https://www.mersenne.org/primes/ |access-date=2026-02-27 |website=www.mersenne.org}}</ref> The 13th, 14th, and 52nd have respectively 157, 183, and 41,024,320 digits.<ref name="www.mersenne.org" /> The largest known primes since 1992 have all been Mersenne primes, with the largest as of 2026 being 2<sup>136,279,841</sup>−1, the 52nd Mersenne prime.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Largest Known prime by Year: A Brief History |url=https://t5k.org/notes/by_year.html |access-date=2026-02-27 |website=t5k.org}}</ref>

==== Mersenne divisors ====
Mersenne divisors are primes that divide 2{{sup|''k''}} − 1, for some prime ''k''. Every Mersenne prime ''p'' is also a Mersenne divisor, with ''k'' = ''p''.

3, 7, 23, 31, 47, 89, 127, 167, 223, 233, 263, 359, 383, 431, 439, 479, 503, 719, 839, 863, 887, 983, 1103, 1319, 1367, 1399, 1433, 1439, 1487, 1823, 1913, 2039, 2063, 2089, 2207, 2351, 2383, 2447, 2687, 2767, 2879, 2903, 2999, 3023, 3119, 3167, 3343 ({{OEIS2C|A122094}})

==== Generalized [[Repunit#Repunit primes|repunit primes]] ====
Of the form (''a''{{sup|''n''}}&nbsp;−&nbsp;1)&nbsp;/&nbsp;(''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1) for fixed integer ''a''.

For ''a'' = 2, these are the Mersenne primes, while for ''a'' = 10 they are the [[#Repunit primes|repunit primes]].  For other small ''a'', they are given below:

==== Other generalizations and variations ====
Many generalizations of Mersenne primes have been defined.  This include the following:
* Primes of the form {{math|''b<sup>n</sup>'' − (''b'' − 1)<sup>''n''</sup>}},<ref>{{Cite OEIS |A121091|Smallest nexus prime of the form n^p - (n-1)^p, where p is an odd prime}}</ref><ref>{{Cite OEIS |A121616|Primes of form (n+1)^5 - n^5}}</ref><ref>{{Cite OEIS |A121618|Nexus primes of order 7 or primes of form n^7 - (n-1)^7}}</ref> including the Mersenne primes and the [[cuban prime]]s as special cases
* [[Williams prime]]s, of the form {{math|(''b'' − 1)·''b<sup>n</sup>'' − 1}}

=== Residue classes of primes ===
{{main|Dirichlet's theorem on arithmetic progressions}}

Of the form ''an'' + ''d'' for fixed integers ''a'' and ''d''. Also called primes congruent to ''d'' [[Modular arithmetic|modulo]] ''a''.

The primes of the form 2''n''+1 are the odd primes, including all primes other than 2.  Some sequences have alternate names: 4''n''+1 are the Pythagorean primes, 4''n''+3 are the integer Gaussian primes, and 6''n''+5 are the Eisenstein primes (with 2 omitted).  The classes 10''n''+''d'' (''d'' = 1, 3, 7, 9) are primes ending in the decimal digit ''d''.

If ''a'' and ''d'' are relatively prime, the arithmetic progression contains infinitely many primes.

=== Smarandache–Wellin primes ===
{{main|Smarandache–Wellin number}}

Primes that are the concatenation of the first ''n'' primes written in decimal.

The fourth Smarandache-Wellin prime is the 355-digit concatenation of the first 128 primes that end with 719.

=== Solinas primes ===
{{main|Solinas prime}}

Prime of the form <math>f(2^m)</math>, where <math>f(x)</math> is a low-[[degree of a polynomial|degree]] [[polynomial]] with small [[integer]] [[coefficient]]s.

* [[3]], [[5]], [[7]], [[11 (number)|11]], [[13 (number)|13]] ({{OEIS2C|A165255}}; primes of the form <math>2^a\pm2^b\pm1</math>)
* 2{{sup|32}}&nbsp;−&nbsp;5, the largest prime that fits into 32 bits of memory.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Primes just less than a power of two 8 to 100 bits (page 1 of 4) |url=https://t5k.org/lists/2small/0bit.html |access-date=2025-08-19 |website=t5k.org}}</ref>
* 2{{sup|64}}&nbsp;−&nbsp;59, the largest prime that fits into 64 bits of memory.

=== Wall–Sun–Sun primes ===
{{main|Wall–Sun–Sun prime}}

A prime ''p''&nbsp;>&nbsp;5, if ''p''{{sup|2}} divides the [[Fibonacci number]] <math>F_{p - \left(\frac{{p}}{{5}}\right)}</math>, where the [[Legendre symbol]] <math>\left(\frac{{p}}{{5}}\right)</math> is defined as
:<math>\left(\frac{p}{5}\right) = \begin{cases} 1 &\textrm{if}\;p \equiv \pm1 \pmod 5\\ -1 &\textrm{if}\;p \equiv \pm2 \pmod 5. \end{cases}</math>

{{As of|2022}}, no Wall-Sun-Sun primes have been found below <math>2^{64}</math> (about <math>18\cdot 10^{18}</math>).<ref>[https://www.primegrid.com/server_status_subprojects.php Subproject status] at PrimeGrid</ref>
